---
title: "Color quadrants: a decision inside a decision"
---

![The color quadrants program: four colored quarters, and a message box in the center that names the clicked color.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0030-Conditions/color-quadrants.png){width=360}

The second decision program looks like a close relative of the first
one, and it is: the canvas is now split into four colored quadrants, and
a click anywhere makes a black box in the center announce the color's
name. But there is a twist hiding in the geometry. Three stripes could
be sorted with questions about `mouseX` alone. Four quadrants can't:
this time, no single question about one coordinate can tell all four
areas apart.

## AI tutor {#sec-tutor-color-quadrants}

An if statement inside another one is where many beginners lose track of which
branch runs when. The AI tutor of this part walks through your decision with
you, condition by condition.

{{< tutor tutor-conditions >}}

## Two questions, four answers {#sec-two-questions}

Think about how you would decide as a human. Someone points at a spot on
the canvas, and you want to name the quadrant. You'd naturally ask two
questions, one after the other: is the spot in the left half or the
right half? And is it in the upper half or the lower half? Two
questions, each with two possible answers, gives two times two, four
combinations, and that's exactly one combination per quadrant.

The first question is a comparison you could write immediately:
`mouseX < width / 2`. The second one is its twin on the other axis:
`mouseY < height / 2`. What's new is how the two questions work
together: the second question is only asked *after* the first one is
answered, inside the branch that the first answer picked.

## An if statement inside an if statement {#sec-nested-if}

Here's the key insight that makes this possible: the block of an if
statement can contain *any* statements, and that includes other if
statements. Putting one if statement inside another is called
**nesting**. The whole decision looks like this:

```typescript
if (mouseX < width / 2) {
  // Left half
  if (mouseY < height / 2) {
    message = "Orange";
  } else {
    message = "Blue";
  }
} else {
  // Right half
  if (mouseY < height / 2) {
    message = "Green";
  } else {
    message = "Red";
  }
}
```

The outer if statement splits the canvas into left and right. Each of
its two branches contains a complete inner if statement that splits its
half into top and bottom. Four leaves at the end, one for each quadrant:

![The nested decision as a tree: the first question picks a half, the
second question picks the quadrant within that
half.](images/quadrant-tree.svg){width=460}

Play computer with one click before you code. Say the canvas is 400 by
200 and the click lands at (300, 60). The outer condition asks: is 300
smaller than 200? No, so the whole first block is skipped and the
program enters the `else` branch. There, the inner condition asks: is
60 smaller than 100? Yes, so `message` becomes `"Green"`. Two questions
answered, one quadrant found.

Watch the indentation as the nesting grows: the inner if statement is
indented one step, its blocks two steps. Every opening brace pushes the
code one step to the right, every closing brace comes back one step.
Without that discipline, nested code becomes a riddle; with it, you can
see the structure of the decision at a glance.

::: {.callout-note}
## Couldn't I ask both questions at once?
You might feel that "left half *and* upper half" should be a single
condition, and you're right: TypeScript can combine two comparisons
into one question. Those combining operators are worth their own
chapters, and they're coming: the first one appears with the bouncing
ball, the second one in the binary guesser project.
:::

## The message box in the center {#sec-center-box}

One more difference to the color areas: the message box now sits in the
middle of the canvas, on top of the quadrant boundaries. Its position
is a centering job, and you know the formula from the responsive robot:
the box's corner sits half the box's width left of the canvas center,
and half its height above it. Give the box its size as two constants,
for example `textAreaWidth` and `textAreaHeight`, and use them both for
drawing the box in `setup` and for clearing it in `mouseClicked`, so
the previous message disappears before the new one is written.

## Your exercise: Color quadrants {#sec-quadrants-exercise}

The color areas chapter walked you through the code. This time the
logic is yours to build; the previous chapter is your reference if you
get stuck.

1. **Paper first.** Draw the 400 by 200 canvas on graph paper, split it
   into quadrants, and label the boundary lines with their formulas
   (`width / 2`, `height / 2`) and values. Assign each quadrant one of
   your four colors.
2. **Play computer on paper.** Pick one test click per quadrant, for
   example (50, 50), (350, 50), (350, 150), and (50, 150). For each,
   walk through your two questions and write down the expected message.
3. **Set the stage in `setup`.** Draw the four quadrants as rectangles
   and the black message box centered on the canvas.
4. **Write `mouseClicked`.** Clear the message box, set up the text
   formatting, then write the nested if statements that fill `message`
   with the name of the clicked color. One `text` statement at the end
   draws it.
5. **Test against your notes.** Click your four test spots and compare
   with the predictions. Then click close to the quadrant boundaries,
   including right near the center where all four quadrants meet.
